Short case 18 · General Surgery

Varicocele

Nine out of ten are on the left, and the reason is pure anatomy. The examiner will want that reason, the fertility figures, and the one circumstance in which a varicocele is a sign of something far worse.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1Definition, incidence and the left-sided question

Definition
B&L: "A varicocele is an abnormal dilatation and enlargement of the scrotal venous plexus draining the testis."​B&L 86 · p.1563
Incidence, with all four figures
"Varicoceles are common, affecting 10–20% of adult males. About 90% are left sided." "If a left varicocele is identified, there is a 30–40% probability that it is a bilateral condition." "They are unusual in boys and typically develop during late childhood and adolescence." And the figure that matters most: "Varicoceles occur in around 15–20% of all males but are found in about 40% of infertile males."​B&L 86 · p.1563
SoCommon in the general population, twice as common in infertile men, and if you find one on the left there is a one in three chance the right is involved too.
Why the left, which is the examiner's favourite
B&L gives the anatomical asymmetry: the right testicular vein drains "into the low-pressure inferior vena cava below the right renal vein",​B&L 86 · p.1563 whereas the left drains into the left renal vein. Three consequences follow, and a complete answer gives all three:
1. The left vein is longer, so the column of blood it must support is taller.
2. It joins the left renal vein at a right angle, rather than obliquely into the cava.
3. It drains into a higher-pressure vein, the renal vein, rather than directly into the low-pressure cava.
The anatomy of the plexus
B&L: "The veins draining the testis and the epididymis form the pampiniform plexus. The veins gradually join each other as they traverse the inguinal canal."​B&L 86 · p.1563 So the varicosity you feel in the scrotum is the pampiniform plexus, and the operation is performed where those veins have coalesced.
The one presentation that is an emergency of a different kind A varicocele of sudden onset, on the right, or one that does not decompress when the patient lies down, raises an abdominal or retroperitoneal mass obstructing the testicular vein, classically a renal cell carcinoma invading the renal vein on the left. The reasoning comes straight from the drainage anatomy B&L gives: the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, so a tumour in the renal vein obstructs it.​B&L 86 · p.1563

So the two questions that convert a trivial case into a serious one are: which side, and does it empty on lying flat? A right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele needs imaging of the abdomen, not a scrotal operation.

2Examination

Before you touch the patient The examiner is marking this before you have found anything. Bailey & Love gives it as a sequence: "ensure you have followed appropriate hand hygiene guidance. Introduce yourself and check the patient's name and date of birth. Request presence of a chaperone as appropriate. Explain what you are going to do, obtain verbal consent and ensure that the patient is comfortable."​B&L 35 · p.472 And the standard it is held to: "patients should be treated with respect and dignity, receive a clear explanation of the examination undertaken and be kept as comfortable as possible. A chaperone should be present, especially for intimate examinations."​B&L 21 · p.285

Do it, and be heard doing itWash your hands. Introduce yourself. Say what you want to examine and why, and ask permission. Ask for a chaperone where the examination is intimate. Expose what you need and cover the rest. Warm your hands. Tell the patient what each step will feel like and that they can ask you to stop, examine the tender part last, and watch their face rather than only your hands. Cover them and thank them before you turn to the examiner.

This one is intimate, so the chaperone is not a courtesy B&L's wording is "especially for intimate examinations", and it adds that this "should be part of a local guideline or policy".​B&L 21 · p.285 Offer a chaperone whatever your sex and the patient's, say that you have offered, and say you would record it. For a child, explain it to the child and ask the parent. If consent is refused, say that you would explain again, offer a chaperone, document the refusal, and not proceed. Examiners ask what you would do if she declined, and that is the whole answer.
Examine standing, then lying
Like any venous lesion, a varicocele fills against gravity, so it is seen and felt standing and should decompress on lying down. B&L's illustration is of a large varicocele in a pendulous scrotum, with a coexisting inguinal hernia.​B&L 86 · p.1563
The classical description
A soft, irregular swelling in the upper scrotum behind and above the testis, which has been likened to a bag of worms. It is separate from the testis, which should be palpable normally below it.
Cough impulse
Present, and this matters because it is a shared false positive with hernia. B&L says it plainly in its varicocele section: "there may be a cough impulse", and that the veins empty when the patient lies down.​B&L 86 · p.1563 Its hernia chapter makes the companion point about a different swelling: "a cough impulse can also be appreciated in a saphena varix."​B&L 64 · p.1061
So the sign does not settle anything on its ownA cough impulse is shared by a hernia, a varicocele and a saphena varix, which is why the rest of the examination, and not this sign, tells you which you are holding.
Measure the testis, both sides
Because testicular atrophy on the affected side is one of the accepted indications for repair in an adolescent, and because it is objective evidence of harm.
And examine the abdomen
For a mass, and for a kidney. Particularly if the varicocele is right-sided, of recent onset, or fails to decompress.
How many grades, and what does "grade 3" mean? The two systems use the same numbers for different things A live disagreement with a real trap in it. B&L 86 p.1564 gives four tiers defined by palpability; SRB 26 p.1064 gives four grades defined by size
Bailey & Love
Four tiers, each defined by what you can feel and see, and when: "subclinical: not palpable or visible at rest or during a Valsalva manoeuvre, but can be shown by special tests (Doppler ultrasound studies); grade 1: palpable during Valsalva manoeuvre, but not otherwise; grade 2: palpable at rest, but not visible; grade 3: visible and palpable at rest."​B&L 86 · p.1564 B&L calls this "useful in clinical practice", and it is: every step is something you do at the bedside, and the ladder runs from Doppler-only to visible.
SRB
Four grades defined by size and tortuosity: "(I) Small, (II) Moderate, (III) Large, (IV) Severely tortuous."​SRB 26 · p.1064 Grade IV then carries an operative consequence in SRB's own treatment list: the scrotal approach is reserved for it, because "in case of grade IV, veins have to be excised through this approach."​SRB 26 · p.1064
Where the trap is
Both systems run to four and both use the words "grade 3" or "grade III", but they are not the same patient. A B&L grade 3 varicocele is simply one you can see standing, which may be moderate in size. An SRB grade III is a large one, and SRB has a further grade above it. So "grade 3" on its own carries no agreed meaning, and an examiner who learned one system will hear the other as wrong.
How to answer: name the system before you use it. Offer B&L's palpability ladder first, because it is the one trials and series use and because every rung is an examination finding: "Subclinical, shown only on Doppler. Grade 1, palpable on Valsalva only. Grade 2, palpable at rest. Grade 3, visible at rest." Then add, in one line, that SRB grades by size, small to severely tortuous, and that grade IV is the one taken through a scrotal approach. Do not say a bare "grade 3" without saying whose. And remember that neither grade decides treatment: the testis and the semen analysis do, which is the next box.

3Why it matters: the fertility question

The association, in B&L's figures
Varicoceles occur in around 15 to 20% of all males but are found in about 40% of infertile males.​B&L 86 · p.1563 That is an association, and the direction of causation is what the examiner is probing.
The proposed mechanisms
Raised scrotal temperature from the pooled venous blood, impairing spermatogenesis; venous stasis with hypoxia; and reflux of adrenal metabolites down the left testicular vein from the renal vein. Testicular atrophy on the affected side is the visible end point.
And the honest position
The association is strong, the mechanism is plausible, and the evidence that repair improves live birth rates is weaker than the evidence that it improves semen parameters. So the defensible answer is: repair for symptoms, for testicular atrophy in an adolescent, and in a man being investigated for infertility with abnormal semen parameters and a palpable varicocele, rather than for every varicocele that is found.

4Investigations

Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler
Confirms the dilated plexus and demonstrates reflux; B&L shows the Doppler ultrasound of a left varicocele.​B&L 86 · p.1563 It also measures testicular volume, which is the objective evidence of harm.
Semen analysis
Where fertility is the issue, before and after any intervention. The numbers that justify operating are the semen parameters, not the size of the varicocele.
Imaging of the abdomen
For a right-sided varicocele, a sudden-onset varicocele, or one that does not decompress on lying down: ultrasound or CT of the abdomen to exclude a retroperitoneal or renal mass obstructing the testicular vein. The anatomy that makes this necessary is the drainage of the left testicular vein into the left renal vein.​B&L 86 · p.1563

5Treatment

When to leave it alone
Most varicoceles. They affect 10 to 20% of all adult men and the majority cause neither symptoms nor infertility.​B&L 86 · p.1563 Reassurance and scrotal support are enough.
When to repair
Pain or a dragging sensation not relieved by support; testicular atrophy, particularly in an adolescent; and infertility with abnormal semen parameters and a palpable varicocele.
How: B&L's order of preference
"When the discomfort is significant, then percutaneous embolisation of the gonadal veins is the usual first-line intervention. If this is not possible, or if the varicocele recurs (as it does in around 20% after embolisation), surgical ligation of the testicular veins is the appropriate treatment."​B&L 86 · p.1564 Among the operations, B&L is explicit: "current evidence indicates that microsurgical varicocelectomy is the most effective method among the different surgical varicocelectomy techniques, with fewer complications and lower recurrence rates."​B&L 86 · p.1564 So: embolise first, operate on the failures, and when you operate, do it under the microscope.
How: SRB's list of approaches, which is what an Indian paper asks for
SRB gives the operations by anatomical level, high to low, and no interventional option at all:​SRB 26 · p.1064
Palomo's operation, suprainguinal extraperitoneal ligation of the testicular vein. Highest, so one or two veins only, but the artery lies alongside them.
Inguinal approach, Ivanissevich, which SRB calls "easier and safer".
Subinguinal approach, Marc Goldstein, "at superficial inguinal ring outside the external oblique aponeurosis without opening the external oblique aponeurosis", so the cord is reached through a small incision without dividing the aponeurosis. This is the level at which microsurgical repair is done.
Scrotal approach, reserved for grade IV, where the veins have to be excised.
Laparoscopic, which SRB marks as accepted but controversial.
RecurrenceSRB gives 5 to 10% after surgery.​SRB 26 · p.1064 B&L gives around 20% after embolisation.​B&L 86 · p.1564 Those are two different operations, not two estimates of one.
What improves, and how fast
SRB: "oligospermia, usually in 6–12 weeks oligospermia improves very well and also the conception rate."​SRB 26 · p.1064 B&L is more guarded, and the amber box below sets out why that matters.
The complications to name
Recurrence, from missed collateral veins; hydrocele, from ligation of the lymphatics, which is the commonest complication of non-microsurgical techniques; and testicular atrophy, from injury to the testicular artery. Preserving the artery and the lymphatics is what the microsurgical technique is for.​B&L 86 · p.1564
Embolise or operate, and does repair actually improve fertility? A live disagreement about both the first move and the claim. B&L 86 p.1564 puts embolisation first and hedges the fertility benefit; SRB 26 p.1064 offers only operations and states the benefit flatly
Bailey & Love
Radiology first: "percutaneous embolisation of the gonadal veins is the usual first-line intervention", with surgery kept for failure or recurrence, which it puts at around 20% after embolisation.​B&L 86 · p.1564 On fertility it cites the trial evidence and then restricts the indication: a 2012 Cochrane review "concluded that there is some evidence to suggest that treatment of a varicocele in men from couples with otherwise unexplained subfertility may improve a couple's chance of spontaneous pregnancies. However, varicocele repair in men with a subclinical varicocele or normal semen parameters is considered ineffective for increasing the chances of spontaneous pregnancies."​B&L 86 · p.1564 It also warns the other way for the young: "treatment of varicocele in adolescents poses a risk of overtreatment: most boys with a varicocele will have no fertility problems later in life."​B&L 86 · p.1564 And it concedes the central uncertainty outright: "the exact association between reduced male fertility and varicocele is unknown."​B&L 86 · p.1564
SRB
Five operative approaches and no embolisation anywhere in the chapter.​SRB 26 · p.1064 It calls the infertility "correctable infertility"​SRB 26 · p.1063 and lists among the benefits of surgery that "usually in 6–12 weeks oligospermia improves very well and also the conception rate."​SRB 26 · p.1064 SRB does not leave this unqualified, though. In its own note it concedes "it is a debate whether it really causes subfertility" before listing the proposed mechanisms.​SRB 26 · p.1064 So SRB contains both positions, the confident one in the treatment list and the cautious one in the note.
Why they differ, which is the answer to give
Not a disagreement about physiology. Embolisation needs an interventional radiology service with gonadal-vein experience, which is not uniformly available, and SRB is written for a setting where the operation is the realistic option. And the two books are answering different questions: B&L asks what the trials show about live births, SRB asks what happens to the sperm count. Semen parameters do improve after repair far more reliably than pregnancy rates do, so both statements can be true at once.
How to answer: state the indication before the technique, because that is where the marks are. "Most varicoceles need no treatment. I would intervene for pain not relieved by scrotal support, for testicular atrophy, or for a man with a palpable varicocele, abnormal semen parameters and otherwise unexplained subfertility. Repair of a subclinical varicocele, or of a varicocele with normal semen parameters, does not improve the chance of pregnancy." Then give the technique both ways: "Bailey and Love makes percutaneous embolisation first-line, with surgery for the roughly 20% that recur. Where embolisation is not available, subinguinal microsurgical varicocelectomy, the Marc Goldstein level, is the operation of choice because it preserves the testicular artery and lymphatics and so has the lowest rates of recurrence and of post-operative hydrocele." For an Indian written paper, name SRB's approaches high to low, Palomo, Ivanissevich, Marc Goldstein, scrotal, laparoscopic. If asked whether repair cures infertility, say semen parameters improve more reliably than pregnancy rates, and that the association itself is still not fully explained.

6Rapid-fire viva

Define a varicocele and give its incidence.

An abnormal dilatation and enlargement of the scrotal venous plexus draining the testis. It affects 10 to 20% of adult males, about 90% are left sided, and if a left varicocele is found there is a 30 to 40% probability the condition is bilateral. They are unusual in boys and typically develop in late childhood and adolescence.​B&L 86 · p.1563

Why are 90% left sided?

Because of the drainage asymmetry. The right testicular vein drains into the low-pressure inferior vena cava below the right renal vein, whereas the left drains into the left renal vein.​B&L 86 · p.1563 So on the left the vein is longer, supporting a taller column of blood; it joins at a right angle rather than obliquely; and it drains into a higher-pressure vein rather than directly into the cava.

What is the relationship with infertility?

Varicoceles occur in around 15 to 20% of all males but are found in about 40% of infertile males.​B&L 86 · p.1563 That is a strong association; the proposed mechanisms are raised scrotal temperature from pooled venous blood impairing spermatogenesis, venous stasis with hypoxia, and reflux of adrenal metabolites down the left testicular vein. But the evidence that repair improves live birth rates is weaker than the evidence that it improves semen parameters, so I would repair for symptoms, for testicular atrophy in an adolescent, or for infertility with abnormal semen parameters and a palpable varicocele, rather than for every varicocele found.

A right-sided varicocele of recent onset. What are you worried about?

An abdominal or retroperitoneal mass obstructing the testicular vein. The anatomy makes this logical: the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein and the right into the cava,​B&L 86 · p.1563 so a new varicocele on the unusual side, or one that fails to decompress on lying down, suggests obstruction rather than simple valvular incompetence, classically renal cell carcinoma invading the renal vein. Image the abdomen rather than operating on the scrotum.

Which veins are involved?

The pampiniform plexus, formed by the veins draining the testis and epididymis, which gradually join each other as they traverse the inguinal canal.​B&L 86 · p.1563 That coalescence is why a high ligation can control the varicocele with few vessels, and why missed collaterals cause recurrence.

A groin and scrotal swelling with a cough impulse. Is it a hernia?

Not necessarily. A varicocele gives a cough impulse, as does a saphena varix, and both are referred as suspected inguinal hernias.​B&L 64 · p.1061​Das 38 · p.599 Look for an expansile impulse, for reducibility, and for whether you can get above the swelling: you can get above a varicocele and feel normal cord above it, and it decompresses on lying down.

How would you grade a varicocele?

Say whose system you are using, because the two books use the same numbers differently. Bailey and Love grades by palpability: subclinical, shown only on Doppler; grade 1, palpable on Valsalva only; grade 2, palpable at rest but not visible; grade 3, visible and palpable at rest.​B&L 86 · p.1564 SRB grades by size: I small, II moderate, III large, IV severely tortuous.​SRB 26 · p.1064 Neither grade decides treatment; the testicular volume and the semen analysis do.

When would you operate?

For pain or a dragging sensation not relieved by scrotal support; for testicular atrophy, particularly in an adolescent; and for infertility with abnormal semen parameters and a palpable varicocele. Not for an incidental asymptomatic varicocele with normal semen parameters, since 10 to 20% of all men have one.​B&L 86 · p.1563

What operations are available, and which is preferred?

Microsurgical subinguinal or inguinal varicocelectomy, laparoscopic high ligation, open retroperitoneal high ligation by the Palomo approach, and radiological embolisation of the testicular vein. Bailey and Love notes varicocelectomy techniques with fewer complications and lower recurrence rates,​B&L 86 · p.1564 and the microsurgical approach is generally preferred because individual veins can be ligated while preserving the testicular artery and the lymphatics.

What are the complications of varicocele repair?

Recurrence, from missed collateral veins; hydrocele, from ligating the lymphatics, which is the commonest complication of non-microsurgical techniques; and testicular atrophy, from injury to the testicular artery. Preserving the artery and lymphatics is precisely what the microsurgical technique achieves.​B&L 86 · p.1564

Why examine the patient standing?

Because a varicocele is a venous lesion that fills against gravity, so it is best seen and felt standing and should decompress on lying down. Bailey and Love's illustration is of a large varicocele in a pendulous scrotum.​B&L 86 · p.1563 Failure to decompress on lying flat is the finding that should send you to image the abdomen.

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love, the testis and scrotum are chapter 86. The books conflict twice here, and both disagreements are set out in the amber boxes: they grade the varicocele on different axes using the same numbers, and they disagree on whether the first intervention is radiological or operative. Alongside those, note the four incidence figures and the drainage asymmetry, which between them answer most of what else can be asked.
